A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Red-Bandit and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–E. The complete documents support reliable comparison despite substantial layout changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original AdvBench attack results, component ablations, attack-style distributions, and the HarmBench reward-design experiment in Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a HarmBench comparison across six target-model configurations in Table 3.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.3 newly proposes optional supervised fine-tuning before expert RL to improve style conditioning in custom domains. SFT already appeared in v1's separate Appendix B reward-design experiment, so this extends its stated role rather than introducing an entirely new technique. The GRPO loss, safety rewards, ten LoRA experts, and bandit routing remain unchanged.

E1.justification: v2 adds HH-Harmless as a training source for its new main-text HarmBench comparison, using 500 selected behaviors. HarmBench itself was already evaluated in v1 Appendix B; AdvBench, the existing training corpora, and the red-teaming task remain covered.

E2.justification: v2 Table 3 introduces reported comparisons against PAIR and TAP, which v1 discussed but did not include in results. It also compares against GCG-Universal and AutoDAN-Universal on HarmBench. This substantially expands comparison with iterative attack methods; the AdvBench comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added HarmBench experiment introduces a separate protocol: 500 HH-Harmless training behaviors filtered by CLIP cosine similarity at a 0.2 threshold, HarmBench-cls scoring, 10- and 20-query budgets, and six 7B/13B/14B target configurations. The existing AdvBench protocol and Appendix B's overlap-disclosing reward study remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The RL/bandit component ablation, reward-design ablation, attack-style distribution analysis, generated examples, and GPT-4o evaluation failure case are retained. The added HarmBench comparison does not introduce a separate ablation or robustness study.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2 retains point-estimate reporting; its added discussion of bandit confidence and convergence does not add empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: v2 Table 3 adds HarmBench scores for both bandit policies at 10 and 20 queries across six targets, alongside four baselines. For example, UCB ASR@20 is 85.0 on Llama2-7B and 70.5 on Qwen-7B. These are newly reported experimental conditions, not improvements over matched v1 scores. All matched AdvBench, style-distribution, and ablation table values remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The red-teaming objective and Equations (1)–(3), including the loss, advantage estimate, and regret definition, are unchanged. v2 mentions sample-complexity bounds and convergence qualitatively but supplies no new explicit bound, theorem, derivation, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list extend the empirical superiority claim from AdvBench to AdvBench and HarmBench. Section 6.1 additionally asserts superiority over Atoxia under single-query constraints given sufficient exploration. The central contributions of style-specific LoRA experts, bandit adaptation, and vulnerability diagnosis remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments about modular experts' scalability relative to monolithic training, bandit convergence under larger query budgets, and independent evaluation as evidence against reward hacking. It explicitly discusses insufficient exploration and SFT needs in custom domains. The earlier future directions involving style composition and partial gray-box access are removed.

D1.justification: v2 documents the new training subset's source, size, CLIP representation, and cosine-similarity cutoff. Appendix C retains the same optimization settings, LoRA parameters, decoding configuration, hyperparameter sweeps, precision, and A100 hardware information. No new code-access information is supplied.

R1.justification: v2 adds FLIRT to related work, explicitly connects bandit routing to test-time adaptation through additional citations, and cites the HH-Harmless and CLIP sources. The existing positioning against prompt optimization, search, RL attackers, and SoC remains largely intact.

P1.justification: v2 reorganizes the experimental subsections around AdvBench and HarmBench, revises the discussion, removes the separate Future Work subsection and duplicated diagnostic discussion, and changes numerical citations to author–date citations. Most existing exposition and appendix text are retained.

P2.justification: The document changes from predominantly single-column to two-column formatting, with extensive reflow of text, equations, references, and floats. v2 adds the HarmBench table, relocates Figure 1 and several existing tables, and resizes displays. The two pipeline diagrams and existing appendix displays retain their substantive content.

improvement.justification: The added classifier-scored HarmBench comparison, filtered HH-Harmless training set, and PAIR/TAP comparisons strengthen empirical support beyond v1's keyword-based comparisons and overlap-affected appendix study. The gain is tempered by unclear per-baseline query budgets and new claims about unbiased evaluation, reward hacking, and sample-complexity-based performance that exceed the supplied evidence. Overall, v2 provides better validation, but the improvement in evidential quality is limited.
